prompt: Which modification of Experiment 1 would allow the experimenters to test the effect of the volume of acid in the flask on the volume of base needed?

choices.text: Measure the volume of acid in the flask in each trial of Experiment 1 instead of measuring the volume of base needed
choices.rationale: Measuring the volume of acid in the flask does not test its effect; it must be deliberately varied.

choices.text: Vary both the volume of acid in the flask and the concentration of the acid at the same time in each trial, measuring the volume of base needed
choices.rationale: Changing two factors at once makes it impossible to tell which one caused any change.

choices.text: Vary the volume of acid in the flask while holding the concentration of the acid and all other conditions constant
choices.rationale: Correct. To test a new factor, change only that factor and hold everything else, including the original independent variable, constant.

choices.text: Repeat Experiment 1 exactly as before, but with a larger number of values of the concentration of the acid
choices.rationale: This gives more detail about acid concentration but never changes the volume of acid in the flask.

explanation: A fair test of the volume of acid in the flask changes it alone. The concentration of the acid, which was the variable in Experiment 1, must now be held fixed.

table.caption: Experiment 1: Students placed 25 mL of an acid solution of known concentration in a flask with a few drops of indicator and added base solution from a burette, swirling, until the indicator changed color. They recorded the volume of base added. Table 1 lists the results.

prompt: Based on Experiments 1 and 2, is the claim that the stirring rate affects the mass of salt that dissolved supported?

choices.text: Yes; the mass of salt that dissolved increased as water temperature increased in both experiments
choices.rationale: That trend concerns water temperature, not the stirring rate, and appears identically in both experiments.

choices.text: No; at every water temperature tested, the two experiments gave the same mass dissolved
choices.rationale: Correct. Changing the condition left every result unchanged, so the results give no sign that it matters.

choices.text: No; the mass of salt that dissolved did not change with water temperature in either experiment
choices.rationale: The mass of salt that dissolved did change with water temperature; the point is that the condition made no difference.

choices.text: Yes; the mass of salt that dissolved was higher for stirred rapidly than for stirred slowly at every water temperature
choices.rationale: The two columns are identical, so neither condition gave higher values.

explanation: Experiments 1 and 2 differ only in the stirring rate, and every value is the same in both, so the results do not support the claim.

table.caption: Experiment 1: Students heated 100 g of distilled water to a set temperature in a beaker stirring slowly and added the salt one gram at a time, stirring after each addition, until no more would dissolve. They recorded the total mass dissolved at each temperature. Experiment 2: The procedure was repeated stirring rapidly, with everything else unchanged. Table 1 lists the results of both experiments.

prompt: To decide whether the concentration of dissolved carbon dioxide has an effect on the rate of photosynthesis, a student should compare the results of:

choices.text: Neither experiment, because the light intensity was varied in both of them
choices.rationale: Varying light intensity in both experiments is what makes them comparable row by row; the comparison across experiments is exactly what is needed.

choices.text: Experiment 1 alone, because it tested the full range of the light intensity under one condition
choices.rationale: Experiment 1 used a single setting of the concentration of dissolved carbon dioxide, so by itself it cannot reveal its effect.

choices.text: Experiment 2 alone, because it was the only experiment performed in water with 2.0 g/L of sodium bicarbonate added
choices.rationale: Experiment 2 also used only one setting of the concentration of dissolved carbon dioxide; a comparison is required.

choices.text: Experiments 1 and 2 together, because they differ only in the concentration of dissolved carbon dioxide
choices.rationale: Correct. Only by comparing results obtained under the two conditions, with everything else the same, can the effect of that condition be isolated.

explanation: Each experiment holds the concentration of dissolved carbon dioxide fixed at one setting; the two settings differ between experiments, so comparing Experiments 1 and 2 isolates its effect.

stimulus.title: Light and Photosynthesis
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students placed a sprig of pondweed in a test tube of water in water with 0.5 g/L of sodium bicarbonate added as a source of carbon dioxide and set a lamp at distances giving several light intensities. They counted the oxygen bubbles released in one minute at each intensity, repeating each count three times.
Results (the rate of photosynthesis): at 100 µmol/m²/s, 15.8 bubbles/min; at 200 µmol/m²/s, 21.1 bubbles/min; at 300 µmol/m²/s, 23.7 bubbles/min; at 400 µmol/m²/s, 25.3 bubbles/min; at 500 µmol/m²/s, 26.4 bubbles/min; at 600 µmol/m²/s, 27.1 bubbles/min.

Experiment 2
The procedure of Experiment 1 was repeated in water with 2.0 g/L of sodium bicarbonate added, with everything else unchanged.
Results: at 100 µmol/m²/s, 24.0 bubbles/min; at 200 µmol/m²/s, 32.0 bubbles/min; at 300 µmol/m²/s, 36.1 bubbles/min; at 400 µmol/m²/s, 38.5 bubbles/min; at 500 µmol/m²/s, 40.1 bubbles/min; at 600 µmol/m²/s, 41.2 bubbles/min.

prompt: Suppose Experiment 1 were repeated with a room temperature of 10°C, a setting between those used in Experiments 1 and 2. At a time of 0 h, the voltage of the battery would most likely be:

choices.text: between 1.39 V and 1.61 V
choices.rationale: Correct. At 0 h, Experiment 1 gave 1.61 and Experiment 2 gave 1.39; an intermediate setting should give an intermediate result.

choices.text: between 1.33 V and 1.54 V
choices.rationale: These are the results for 2 h, not 0 h.

choices.text: below both experiments' results, less than 1.39 V
choices.rationale: This is below both experiments' results at this row; an intermediate setting should not fall outside them.

choices.text: above both experiments' results, greater than 1.61 V
choices.rationale: This is above both experiments' results at this row; an intermediate setting should not fall outside them.

explanation: The two experiments bracket the new setting, so the result at 0 h should lie between 1.39 and 1.61 V.

table.caption: Experiment 1: Students connected a fresh AA battery to a small lamp in a room at 20°C and measured the battery's voltage with a voltmeter at regular intervals while the lamp stayed on. Experiment 2: The procedure was repeated in a cold room at 0°C, with everything else unchanged. Table 1 lists the results of both experiments.

prompt: Which of the following is the most serious flaw in the procedure of Experiment 1?

choices.text: The height from which the water was poured changed between trials, confounding the effect of the slope angle of the tray
choices.rationale: Correct. A second factor that changes along with the independent variable confounds the results.

choices.text: Only a single value of the slope angle of the tray was tested, so no trend could possibly be identified
choices.rationale: The results list 5 different values of slope angle.

choices.text: The mass of soil eroded was measured in every trial rather than only in the final trial of the series
choices.rationale: The dependent variable must be measured in every trial.

choices.text: The slope angle of the tray was deliberately changed from trial to trial instead of being held constant throughout
choices.rationale: Changing the independent variable is the point of the experiment, not a flaw.

explanation: Good design changes only slope angle. Because the height from which the water was poured also changed, any difference in soil eroded could be due to either factor.

stimulus.title: Slope and Soil Erosion
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students filled identical trays with 5 kg of the same soil, tilted each tray to a set angle, and sprinkled water evenly over it from a watering can. They collected the soil that washed out of the tray, dried it, and found its mass. The experimenters did not keep the height from which the water was poured the same from one trial to the next.
Results (the mass of soil eroded): at 5°, 42 g; at 10°, 106 g; at 15°, 193 g; at 20°, 302 g; at 25°, 434 g.

prompt: Based on Experiment 1 alone, which of the following statements goes beyond what the data can support?

choices.text: The sound intensity would keep decreasing beyond 6 m.
choices.rationale: Correct. No trials were run beyond 6 m, so the results cannot show what happens there.

choices.text: The sound intensity at 3 m was more than twice its value at 5 m.
choices.rationale: This statement is directly supported by the listed results.

choices.text: The sound intensity at 1 m was more than twice its value at 3 m.
choices.rationale: This statement is directly supported by the listed results.

choices.text: The sound intensity at 3 m was more than twice its value at 6 m.
choices.rationale: This statement is directly supported by the listed results.

explanation: Three of the statements can be checked against the table and hold. "The sound intensity would keep decreasing beyond 6 m." cannot: no trials were run beyond 6 m, so the results cannot show what happens there.

table.caption: Experiment 1: In an open field, students placed a speaker playing a steady tone and used a sound meter to measure the intensity at several distances along a straight line from the speaker. Readings were taken at the same height above the ground. Table 1 lists the results.

prompt: To determine whether the kind of seed influences the height of the seedlings, the experimenters should most likely:

choices.text: Repeat Experiment 1 exactly as before, but with a larger number of values of the fertilizer concentration
choices.rationale: This gives more detail about fertilizer concentration but never changes the kind of seed.

choices.text: Vary both the kind of seed and the fertilizer concentration at the same time in each trial, measuring the height of the seedlings
choices.rationale: Changing two factors at once makes it impossible to tell which one caused any change.

choices.text: Vary the kind of seed while holding the fertilizer concentration and all other conditions constant
choices.rationale: Correct. To test a new factor, change only that factor and hold everything else, including the original independent variable, constant.

choices.text: Measure the kind of seed in each trial of Experiment 1 instead of measuring the height of the seedlings

table.caption: Experiment 1: Students planted bean seeds in identical pots of potting soil and watered each pot with 100 mL of fertilizer solution every other day. After 4 weeks they measured the height of each seedling. Each concentration was tested with five pots, and the average height was recorded. Table 1 lists the results.

choices.text: No; the period of the pendulum did not change with string length in either experiment

table.caption: Experiment 1: Students hung a metal bob from a string using a 50 g bob, pulled the bob 10° to one side, and released it. They timed 10 complete swings with a stopwatch and divided by 10 to find the period. The procedure was repeated for several string lengths. Experiment 2: The procedure was repeated using a 100 g bob, with everything else unchanged. Table 1 lists the results of both experiments.

prompt: Which experiment(s) provide the information needed to determine whether the temperature of the solution affects the time for the reaction to finish?

choices.text: Neither experiment, because the mass of catalyst was varied in both of them
choices.rationale: Varying catalyst mass in both experiments is what makes them comparable row by row; the comparison across experiments is exactly what is needed.

choices.text: Experiments 1 and 2 together, because they differ only in the temperature of the solution
choices.rationale: Correct. Only by comparing results obtained under the two conditions, with everything else the same, can the effect of that condition be isolated.

choices.text: Experiment 2 alone, because it was the only experiment performed in a water bath at 30°C
choices.rationale: Experiment 2 also used only one setting of the temperature of the solution; a comparison is required.

choices.text: Experiment 1 alone, because it tested the full range of the mass of catalyst under one condition

stimulus.title: Catalyst and Reaction Time
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students mixed 50 mL of hydrogen peroxide solution from a single bottle with a measured mass of powdered catalyst in a water bath at 20°C and timed how long it took for the bubbling to stop.
Results (the time for the reaction to finish): at 0 mg, 186 s; at 2 mg, 111 s; at 4 mg, 71 s; at 6 mg, 49 s; at 8 mg, 37 s.

Experiment 2
The procedure of Experiment 1 was repeated in a water bath at 30°C, with everything else unchanged.
Results: at 0 mg, 102 s; at 2 mg, 61 s; at 4 mg, 39 s; at 6 mg, 27 s; at 8 mg, 20 s.

table.caption: Experiment 1: Students placed 25 mL of an acid solution of known concentration in a flask with a few drops of indicator using a 0.10 M base solution and added base solution from a burette, swirling, until the indicator changed color. They recorded the volume of base added. Experiment 2: The procedure was repeated using a 0.20 M base solution, with everything else unchanged. Table 1 lists the results of both experiments.

prompt: The design of Experiment 1 has a weakness. Which statement best describes it?

choices.text: The altitude of the station was deliberately changed from trial to trial instead of being held constant throughout
choices.rationale: Changing the independent variable is the point of the experiment, not a flaw.

choices.text: The heating method changed between trials, confounding the effect of the altitude of the station
choices.rationale: Correct. A second factor that changes along with the independent variable confounds the results.

choices.text: The boiling point of the water was measured in every trial rather than only in the final trial of the series
choices.rationale: The dependent variable must be measured in every trial.

choices.text: Only a single value of the altitude of the station was tested, so no trend could possibly be identified
choices.rationale: The results list 6 different values of altitude.

explanation: Good design changes only altitude. Because the heating method also changed, any difference in boiling point could be due to either factor.

stimulus.title: Altitude and Boiling Point
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
A team carried the same kettle, thermometer, and a measured volume of distilled water to stations at several altitudes. At each station the water was heated until it boiled steadily and the temperature was recorded. Because of limited equipment, the heating method was different for each trial.
Results (the boiling point of the water): at 0 m, 100.0 °C; at 500 m, 98.3 °C; at 1000 m, 96.5 °C; at 1500 m, 94.8 °C; at 2000 m, 93.1 °C; at 2500 m, 91.4 °C.

table.caption: Experiment 1: A testing company fitted new tires of one model to the same car and measured the tread depth with a gauge after each 10,000 km of driving on a fixed route. Table 1 lists the results.
